books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: Henry Highland Garnet, “An Address to the Slaves of the United States,” 1843

stimulus.text:
"Brethren, arise, arise! Strike for your lives and liberties. Now is the day and the hour. . . . Rather die freemen than live to be slaves. Remember that you are FOUR MILLIONS!" — Henry Highland Garnet, "An Address to the Slaves of the United States," National Negro Convention, Buffalo, New York, August 1843.

"Right is of no Sex—Truth is of no Color—God is the Father of us all, and we are all brethren." — Motto of The North Star, Frederick Douglass’s newspaper, first issue, December 3, 1847.

The convention refused to endorse Garnet’s address, by a single vote, and Douglass spoke against it.
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotations: Henry Highland Garnet, “An Address to the Slaves of the United States,” National Negro Convention, Buffalo, August 1843; motto of The North Star, first issue, December 3, 1847. Wording checked against BlackPast and the Library of Congress.

source: original; stimuli are verbatim public-domain quotations from Garnet (1843) and The North Star (1847)
stem: The convention refused to endorse Garnet’s address by a single vote, with Douglass speaking against it. That rejection best shows that Black abolitionists

options.misconception: All sides at the convention opposed slavery; they differed on tactics.

options.text: were divided over whether Black people should leave America
options.misconception: The vote was about Garnet’s call to rise, not about emigration.

options.text: disagreed about tactics while sharing the goal of ending slavery

options.misconception: Douglass had broken with Garrison and founded his own paper.

rationales.A: No one at the convention defended slavery. The argument was over how to end it, not whether to end it.
rationales.B: Emigration was not on the ballot. The vote decided whether to endorse Garnet’s call for enslaved people to rise.
rationales.C: Garnet urged rising; Douglass spoke against endorsing it. One goal, two tactics, decided by a single vote.
rationales.D: Douglass did not follow Garrison without question. He had broken with him and founded the North Star.
rationales.general:
1. Note what the vote decided. It refused to endorse a call to rise, by one vote.
2. Note who opposed it. Douglass, a leading Black abolitionist, spoke against it.
3. Name the lesson. One movement can hold one goal and argue hard over how to reach it.
Background: The 1843 convention met in Buffalo, and Garnet’s address failed endorsement by a single vote.
Remember: a close vote is evidence of a real argument, not of a broken movement.
